query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, alumina‐forming surface coating (e.g., an aluminide coating) to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will significantly reduce its oxygen uptake and pesting when exposed to air at high temperatures while largely preserving its room‐temperature ductility and high‐temperature strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy with known room-temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) and yield strength at elevated temperature.
generation.intervention: Deposition of a thin, adherent aluminide coating that promotes the in situ formation of a continuous Al2O3 scale on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at approximately 800 °C for 5 hours, with mechanical loading conditions similar to those used in prior mechanical tests (strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, slow-growing Al2O3 (alumina) scale on the alloy’s surface.
generation.mechanism: The aluminide coating oxidizes preferentially, forming a stable, adherent alumina layer that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion. This limits internal oxidation and pesting without substantially altering the bulk alloy’s microstructure and, hence, its mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated samples will exhibit significantly improved oxygen resistance (reduced oxidation and no pesting) at 800 °C for at least 5 hours compared to untreated material, while maintaining comparable room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibits inadequate oxygen resistance (pesting/oxidation) under high-temperature exposure in air despite good mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: Temperature around 800 °C, exposure duration of 5 hours in an air atmosphere, and mechanical testing conditions consistent with low strain rates (10^−4–10^−2 s^−1). The hypothesis does not claim performance at substantially higher temperatures, longer exposures, or under drastically different mechanical loads.
generation.uncertainty: The exact long-term stability of the alumina scale under cyclic thermal conditions and its influence on fatigue properties are not established. Additionally, while the coating is designed to minimize interference with bulk mechanical performance, a small degradation cannot be entirely ruled out without comprehensive testing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples: one group with the applied aluminide coating and a control group without coating. Subject both groups to air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours under identical conditions. After exposure, evaluate oxidation behavior (mass gain, oxide layer continuity, presence of pesting) and perform mechanical tests (tensile ductility at room temperature and yield strength at elevated temperature).
measurements: Microstructural characterization of the oxide scale (using SEM/EDS or XRD)
Room-temperature tensile ductility (percentage strain to failure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminide-coated samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in oxygen uptake and suppression of pesting compared to the uncoated control, or if the coating results in a significant degradation of room-temperature or high-temperature mechanical properties, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen
